True story, I swear. But I would like to present Cybernetics in its fullness and its richness as a tradition.

speaker: Paul Pangaro
text: As I say here on the slide, it's a bilingual synthesis. It is both analog and digitally concerned, and in fact, was born at the surge of both analog and digital views of the world. So it encompasses both the organic and the artificial, and indeed, the natural, and technological, and social. How does it do this? It does this because it's grounded in the role of information as feedback to effective action. A system has to have knowledge of its consequences, its actions in the world, in the environment, in order to achieve its purpose and in order to define its own purpose ongoing. So again, just very briefly, I would claim that the rationale for Cybernetics in the world, in science, is because it uniquely approaches systems in terms of purpose. So—If I observe a system and I explain it, then I am looking at it as it's functioning, and I am claiming what I see as how it is operating. But if it's about purpose, then I have to examine *my own purpose* as an *observer* in explaining what the system is. You've heard of this as Second-order Cybernetics and so on.

speaker: Paul Pangaro
text: Of course, it's a kind of self-reflection that is not uncommon in other disciplines—in anthropology, even in management, and so on and so forth. speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: Thank you, Paul. Well, for my opening statement from a cybernetic perspective based on personal research: Paul highlighted which historical time we are located in, and I will start around 1956. I propose to use self-organizing systems as a foundational and invariant theme which runs through the cybernetic tradition to compare and contrast with AI. For that, I will introduce two main characters. One you already heard about: Heinz von Foerster, one of the main protagonists of Cybernetics. But to do that and to highlight self-organizing systems, I also introduce a collaborator of his from Britain, Gordon Pask. ### 1956: A Pivotal Year Around '56, just a couple of years before Pask started his independent cybernetics laboratory in Britain called System Research Ltd.—Cybernetics is on the rise, is *en vogue*, not unlike AI today.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: The summer of '56—and Jill will speak about this in more detail—is, of course, the moment of the Dartmouth AI workshop, which sort of turned Hanover, New Hampshire, into the “Capital of Artificial Intelligence.” That same year, I think about a month later, over in Europe, the First International Congress on Cybernetics is convened in Namur, Belgium, co-organized by Georges Boulanger, a cybernetician who was a professor at the Free University of Brussels (Université Libre de Bruxelles) and at the Faculty of Engineering of the University of Mons. That first International Congress was actually the truly first international event in Cybernetics. At that Congress, the International Association for Cybernetics was co-founded, to which Norbert Wiener was closely related. You could say Namur, Belgium—perhaps not the first city you would think about—was turned into the *“Capital of Cybernetics”* for about 40 years after that, with a long series of these international congresses, always in Namur, and 41 volumes of a journal called *Cybernetica*. By the way, if you want to know a little bit more about that, please reach out after this.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: I did some research on that—it's not very well known, part of the Cybernetics history or canon. Please feel free to reach out. ["M.J.R. van de Wijnckel" \<mike@vandewijnckel.nl>] ### The Biological Computer Laboratory Then we go on to Heinz von Foerster in the US. He co-founds the Biological Computer Laboratory at the University of Illinois, and he thinks, "Okay, I'll attend several international events on Cybernetics to scout collaborators." At the second International Congress on Cybernetics in Namur, Belgium in 1958, he meets Gordon Pask for the first time, which later proves to be a very fruitful encounter. Heinz von Foerster presents his paper there titled, *“Some Aspects in the Design of Biological Computers”,* which is sort of a research agenda program for the BCL. Gordon Pask presents a paper titled *"The Growth Process Inside the Cybernetic Machine."* By the way, these were—at that time, I said Cybernetics was *en vogue*—these were events attended by approximately 1,000 participants. So for today's terms, these were large Cybernetics events.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: Some other notable participants were Ross Ashby, Stafford Beer, Louis Couffignal from France, and Ray Solomonoff, who we will hear about a little bit more in a minute. ### ONR Project: Toward Biological Computers Back at the Biological Computer Lab, it starts with the first large project focused on self-organizing systems. Gordon Pask is onboarded on the team, and Paul has so kindly [put on [a slide of] the final report cover page of that project](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1tj_kEdZuPYcbkG9HR4swYYjI-1poXg58hljKdXxB_E8/edit?slide=id.g3d01b046243_5_45#slide=id.g3d01b046243_5_45), which was titled “*Toward the Realization of Biological Computers."* You see the details and the sponsor: the Office of Naval Research (ONR) at the Information System Branch, Mathematical Science Division, with Heinz von Foerster as the principal investigator. By the way, this is, I think, a very iconic and emblematic lapse regarding "The Split" between Cybernetics and AI at the time.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: Notice that I think the sponsor pre-filled out the title of the report: *"Studies in Artificial Intelligence Computers."* And Heinz von Foerster apparently struck that through—because it's his handwriting—and corrected it to *"Toward the Realization of Biological Computers."* Now I will just quote the principal aim to get a grasp of what it was about [emphasis added to contrast their cybernetic context]: "The principal aim of the study was to develop the conceptual framework, the mathematical tools, and the circuitry and technology for the realization of systems that display biomorphic functions as habituation, adaptation, perception, cognition, recall, learning, memory, abstraction, conceptualization, association, induction, ideation, appetition, awareness, consciousness, self-repair, self-reproduction, growth, evolution, and self-organization. It's an important observation that all these biomorphic functions are meaningless by themselves.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: In order for [biomorphic functions] to become meaningful, it is necessary to stipulate an environment with organizational features, energetically and entropically in close contact with the systems displaying these functions." ### Key Publications Some important publications that came out: Von Foerster (1960): *“Self-Organizing Systems and Their Environments*”—where he solved the apparent paradox of cybernetic self-organizing systems, which apparently were violating the second law of thermodynamics, by showing that the entropic coupling of these systems with their environment actually produces variety-eating systems, or self-organizing systems. Co-authored by Heinz von Foerster and Gordon Pask (1960-61): *"A Predictive Model for Self-Organizing Systems,* *Part One* *and* *Part Two"—*I will come back to those in a minute. ### Cybernetics-AI Encounters During the course of that project, there were also Cybernetics and AI encounters—meeting of minds, so to speak.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: Three years after the Dartmouth split, at the 1959 Interdisciplinary Conference on Self-Organizing Systems, co-sponsored by ONR and the Armour Research Foundation of the Illinois Institute of Technology, important papers there were, again, von Foerster's *“Self-Organizing Systems and Their Environments.”* But also—and that was a nice find, I think, for us in preparation for this meeting—a paper by Newell, Simon, and Shaw titled *"A Variety of Intelligent Learning in a General Problem Solver",* where they give their notion or account of self-organization in the General Problem Solver. ----- ## Summary of Technical Work Now I will move on to summarize hundreds of pages of rather technical and dense papers written by these gentlemen. I will start with a summary from the pair of papers *"A Predictive Model for Self-Organizing Systems" *[*Part One* *and* *Part Two*] by von Foerster and Pask.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: In this paper, which develops a game-theoretical formulation—partly based on hand simulation, partly on the analog computing machine EUCRATES that Paul just showed on screen—von Foerster and Pask model self-organization as a population of players or competing learning automata whose internal connections, external coalitions, and even viability depend on the payoffs they can secure in a shared environment. Their key finding is that persistent or non-trivial self-organization does not arise in a zero-sum competition, but only when the game is non-zero-sum, so that partly cooperative coalitions can form, stabilize, and develop redundant connective structures that give the system memory and resilience. They also show that in a genuinely self-organizing regime, the relevant units are not fixed in advance, but successful elements nucleate, unsuccessful ones disappear, and an observer must continually redraw the system's boundaries to make sense of its behavior. In this way, metastable self-organization appears as an evolving, partly cooperative process that sits between rigid equilibrium and total disintegration. ### Gordon Pask (1964) Now I will take a small jump in time to '64.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: This is a paper where Gordon Pask develops the earlier work in a more formal treatment, and also—which, by the way, he did consistently throughout his career—surveys and reviews developments in Artificial Intelligence. The title of that paper is *"A Discussion of Artificial Intelligence and Self-Organization."* By the way, in the show notes, you will find links to all these papers we're talking about today, so if you want to have a look at those after, you're welcome. Here, Pask shows that if we model learning systems as adaptive automata operating over a fixed set of states or state space, they will eventually converge. They become better adapted, but in doing so, exhaust their capacity for further change. This leads to a fundamental limitation: no such localized system, nor any selection amongst them, can sustain stable self-organization, because optimization drives the system towards a saturated state. Even introducing hierarchies or selection mechanisms or more sophisticated physical implementations—Pask shows that does not resolve anything as long as the system is tied to a fixed structure.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: The key step is to redefine the system itself, not as a finite machine, but as an organization distributed across a medium and maintained through continual self-reproduction and interaction. Such a system of populations of un-localized automata can generate new structures and effectively expand its possibilities, thereby avoiding convergence. In this view, stable, non-trivial self-organization is achieved not by preserving components, but by sustaining a distributed and evolving organization over time. ----- ## From Self-Organization to Conversation Theory Now, to wrap up this notion (Paul, next slide please)... This notion of self-organization gave rise to a coherent lineage of experimental cybernetic research spanning more than half a century, grounded in a strong empirical tradition of adaptive teaching machines and physics. During the '70s, this was formalized into Conversation Theory, together with its dual protologic Lp calculus, during the 1980s. Later it was extended into Interactions of Actors Theory.

speaker: Mike van de Wijnckel
text: In his final paper in 1996, written in honor of Heinz von Foerster, Pask explicitly acknowledges that von Foerster's concept of self-organization had always been the intellectual progenitor of his own work on Conversation Theory—of which you see a hand-drawn diagram here from the '70s, which was directed to Heinz von Foerster. You always see this dual architecture of different players or automata, interacting, conversing, and where all these biomorphic functions that we just reviewed only make sense in that interaction. Heinz von Foerster would say that questions such as "Can machines think or understand, or are they conscious?" is nonsensical, except for in this interaction. And with that, Paul, I give it back to you. -----

speaker: Jill Fain Lehman

Okay, so what's the framing?

speaker: Jill Fain Lehman
text: What do I want to establish as a way to think about what's going on in this moment in time? I'd like to describe it as a change of focus with respect to the role of humans in the core scientific questions each paradigm wants to ask. ### Cybernetics I would say that at this moment in time and well afterward, Cybernetics treats humans as an instance of a self-organizing system with the goal of describing the properties and the behaviors of the full class of self-organizing systems. So at any given point, we should be able to take the pieces that make up the theory—cybernetic theory—and describe or explain or predict things about human behavior because they are members of the class. At the same time, I would argue there are going to be things about humans that the theory doesn't address because it's not within the purview that led to the particular theoretical pieces they're formulating the theory in terms of. ### Artificial Intelligence Now, I want to contrast that with this moment, 1956, and what people are doing in what's going to be called Artificial Intelligence, or AI.

speaker: Jill Fain Lehman
text: I believe AI wants to—at this moment—refocus that conversation to treat humans as THE self-organizing system of concern, and has the goal of describing the properties and behaviors that are specifically necessary for human intelligence. Two different things: - Humans are AN instance of self-organizing systems, but the goal of the theorizing, the goal of the science, is to describe the properties and behaviors of the full class *versus* - Humans are THE self-organizing system of concern, and the goal of the science is to describe the properties and behaviors that are specifically necessary for human intelligence And so, just as with Cybernetics, at any given point we can take the pieces that go into cybernetic theory and predict things about human behavior because humans are an element of the class, in AI, at any given point, we should be able to take the pieces that make up the theories in AI and describe or explain or predict things about intelligent human behavior. Similarly, there are going to be things that the AI theory doesn't cover because of its purview.

speaker: Jill Fain Lehman
text: ----- ## Different Levels of Description So looked at in this way—as this kind of framing—both approaches have things to say about humans, but they're trying to describe regularities that are at different levels of description. And the process of doing science within either theoretical framework is going to get expressed in terms of whatever primitives capture the regularities most easily and most accurately. To the extent that they want to theorize and meet theoretical goals that are fundamentally different, the low-hanging fruit, and then the things that build on the low-hanging fruit once you start to conceptualize in cybernetic or AI frameworks, are going to be different. And there's no guarantee that something that is understood in one framework will be recapitulated early or often in the other framework at all. ----- ## Concrete Examples of AI's Refocusing That's really abstract. So let me just give you two concrete examples of what I mean by AI's refocusing, drawn out of the documents that I mentioned before.

speaker: Jill Fain Lehman
text: ### Example 1: “Neuron Nets” & Abstractions The first and most obvious one comes from, not surprisingly, the Rockefeller Proposal, which lists at the top seven broad categories of stuff that they want to pay attention to and work on over the summer. Oh, by the way, McCarthy says no problem—a bunch of guys can get together for the summer, we're going to make fabulous progress on this. And he does say "guys," basically. So there's no question that all the people there were men—very unlike Cybernetics, which had Margaret Mead and at least a few other women scientists hanging around. We'll just leave that to the side for now. So there's this list of seven general areas, introduced with the following: "These are some aspects of the Artificial Intelligence problem." And number three on the list is “Neuron Nets.” This is the workshop that establishes AI, and here we have it—neuron nets is important enough to go on this list. And what the proposal says is: "How can a set of hypothetical neurons be arranged so as to form concepts?

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: Thanks, Jill. Let me start by saying thank you to both Jill and Paul. This is a remarkable opportunity to step back and reflect on fundamentals in a way that fields rarely do. I think the answer is that the problems they wanted to address seemed to require a different approach.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: They wanted to tackle goal-directed complex information processing— things like problem solving, planning, and complex games like chess—and it wasn't clear how to get there with the available tools of Cybernetics of the day: continuous math, differential equations, the feedback controllers of the time. By the way, "complex information processing" was Newell and Simon's preferred term for the field; they weren't big fans of the term "artificial intelligence." I want to lay out two key issues. One is the topic of inquiry; the second is the role and nature of computation. For Cybernetics of the day, the focus was embedded, goal-directed systems in feedback loops with the environment. For classical AI, the topic of inquiry was complex goal-directed information processing. Cybernetics was distinctive because of what I think of as the ontological primacy of feedback control—it 's feedback loops all the way down, with continuous math and information theory as the principal tools. Computation is there in the background, but it's secondary.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: Classical AI, as launched in the 1950s, was about complex information processing, where computation is primary—and so the principal tool for analysis and engineering is symbolic computation. What Is Computation? I want to contrast the view I'm going to advance—an old view—with a conventional view: that computation is number crunching. A quote from Wiener in 1948 captures this succinctly: computing machines are essentially machines for recording numbers, operating with numbers, and giving the result in numerical form. That's a perfectly sensible view for the time. In the 1940s and 1950s, "computer" was actually a job title—people did numerical calculation. Newell and Simon embraced a quite different view of computation, one envisioned by Ada Lovelace and formalized by Alan Turing.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: Lovelace, writing in the 1840s about Babbage's Analytical Engine, famously wrote that the bounds of arithmetic were outstepped the moment the idea of applying the cards occurred, enabling a mechanism to combine general symbols in successions of unlimited variety and extent—"a uniting link is established between the operations of matter and the most abstract mental processes." In the 1840s, she anticipated two key features of Turing computation: that computation is physical symbol or pattern processing, and that universality is key. Newell reflecting on "The Split" said: "Recall the rhetoric of the '50s, where we insisted that computers were symbol-manipulation machines and not just number-manipulation machines. The mathematicians and engineers then responsible for computers insisted that computers process numbers. On the contrary, we argued that the great thing was that computers could take instructions, and it was incidental, though useful, that they dealt with numbers." An important point: the class of physical symbol- or pattern-processing machines is very broad.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: Herb Simon, in a chapter called "The Patterned Matter That Is Mind," argues persuasively that the patterns arising in artificial neural networks are in fact instances of symbols or patterns in the sense of Newell and Simon's physical symbol system. Computers are pattern crunchers; they can use patterns to represent numbers, not the other way around. Representation & Process What are representations? My take: representations are the internal physical patterns that mediate between sensing and acting in goal-seeking physical pattern-processing machines. In practical systems, representations may be engineered or they may emerge from learning processes. Classical AI was comfortable with engineered representations; modern AI is decidedly emergentist—the engineer designs not the representations but the architectures and loss functions, so the representations emerge. Rich Sutton, the reinforcement-learning pioneer, expressed what he called the bitter lesson of sixty to seventy years of AI research: that the gains from hand-built representations will be short-lived, and that systems which learn their representations will always do better in the long run.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: Process and representation are intricately linked: no process, no representation. Patterns are representations only in virtue of the processes that operate on them. A set of thousands of punched cards represents a portrait not because of what an observer thinks about it, but because of its relationship to the machine and the processes in the machine. Similarly, Tinkertoys represent the tic-tac-toe board because of the processes that operate on those representations and make the thing actually play tic-tac-toe. One very important way that representation and process can give rise to intelligence goes back at least to Wiener's 1948 book, where he briefly speculates about building a chess-playing machine. Rather than starting with feedback control, he proposes what we would now call bounded heuristic search, which allows internal feedback from prospection to guide behavior. Search, symbols, and pattern processing would become the theoretical foundations for Newell and Simon's approach.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: And search remains foundational to AI today—one of the most high-profile recent successes was AlphaGo, which beat the world champion in Go based on neural nets plus reinforcement learning plus look-ahead search. The Knowledge Level In preparation for laying out the overlapping and distinct domains of AI and Cybernetics, I want to bring in something Allen Newell introduced, called the knowledge level. Knowledge, in Newell's take, is whatever can be ascribed to an agent by an observer such that the agent's behavior can be computed or predicted according to the principle of rationality: if an agent has knowledge that some action will lead to one of its goals, then the agent will select that action. This is how we deal with each other on a daily basis. And knowledge in this view remains forever abstract—it can never actually be in hand. It's a challenging idea, but one that merits returning to today. Overlapping Magisteria Now I'm ready to lay out the final picture. The broadest class of systems is symbol-processing or pattern-processing machines. Inside it are interesting special classes that overlap in interesting ways.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: One important special class is what I'm calling embedded teleological feedback systems—the heart of what Cybernetics is about. There are also universal computing machines, and there are knowledge-level systems: systems for which we can ascribe knowledge and goals and compute their behavior according to the principle of rationality. A little Turing machine that computes the reverse-string function is a pattern-processing machine; it's not a universal computing machine. The humble thermostat is a pattern-processing machine of a certain kind. Python, LISP, C++—your favorite programming languages—are universal computing machines. The human mind, by hypothesis, is a universal computing machine and a knowledge-level system. Interestingly, some of the most high-profile successes in AI—like AlphaGo and Deep Blue—are knowledge-level systems but not universal computing machines, because they have very narrow goals. They do one thing. Where do modern AI systems fit? I think modern large language models lie at a very strange point in this space, and this is where I want to leave you.

speaker: Richard L. Lewis
text: We've constructed powerful universal computing machines—kind of linguistic universal computing machines—with vast amounts of knowledge of a certain kind, but we can't reliably treat them as knowledge-level agents. That's where the difficulty lies. And I think, arguably, we humans are members of another special subclass—self-observing, reflective knowledge-level systems. Thank you.

Now let's move from this specific example to an abstraction.

speaker: Paul Pangaro
text: Say I have three patterns as symbols—a T, a P, and a Q—just an abstraction. This abstraction can make a coherence. There's also the equivalent on the prescriptive side—the execution of a prescription-building procedure that produces a procedure about T in participant A. Each of these six equations produces something that becomes available to the other equations in the entirety. So this is a self-organizing system. It's a model for a single set of relations in a coherence about circle / compass / plane, or in the abstract, T / P / Q. What if we had a second individual?

speaker: Paul Pangaro

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: Okay. Thanks, Paul. I'm very glad to be here. Most of my career has been based on studying machine learning, and in particular I am known, and my students as well, for reinforcement learning, and I want to say a little bit about that. But my roots are really in Cybernetics, so I think it's kind of an interesting story. In fact, I think of myself still as a cyberneticist rather than an AI researcher. Now let me just move something on the screen here. Okay. So, machine learning. Let me say just a few words about it. I tend to distinguish between three different kinds of machine learning, although others will distinguish more than these. One is supervised learning, where the training information consists of labeled examples. You have examples of certain classes, you present these to the learning system, and it tries to incorporate these examples and then generalize to instances that are not in the training set. But the key point is that it's learning from labeled examples.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: Sometimes it's called “learning with a teacher.” Unsupervised learning, sometimes called “learning without a teacher”, is where the training information is just data coming in, and the system, depending on how it's designed, will find patterns in the data. One example is clustering. Things that are near each other, in some sense, are clustered together, versus other clusters in other regions of the space. So there are examples, but they're unlabeled, and the system labels them according to some principle. Various principles are used. What I had been studying is called reinforcement learning, and this has sometimes been called “learning with a critic”, instead of “learning with a teacher.” The critic provides a score for what the system does, and the objective of the learning system is to maximize the score. Of course, one never truly finds the maximum, but the point is to try to increase the scores that are received from the environment. So it's very different from having labeled examples. There are no labeled examples; there are “scored examples”, if you will. Sometimes it's called “learning by trial and error.” In fact, it comes from psychology.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: This is Edward Thorndike, who in the 19th century studied various animals in puzzle boxes. He would put, say, a cat in a box. Food would be seen by the cat outside the box, and the cat would try lots of things and eventually stumble on some way of releasing the door, and it was able to get out. Then he'd put it back in the box, and the next exploration would not last as long. It would discover the way to get out more quickly, and eventually the animal would let itself out immediately. He did this even with fish. I'm not quite sure how he did this with fish. So the animal tried things and finally found something that succeeded, and then remembered that. "Trial and error" is not the right term, because trial and error is not error correction. That's a confusing term, so I think it should be trial and evaluation rather than trial and error. Anyway, Thorndike came up with what is now called the law of effect. Basically it's this common-sense idea that if you do something and it's followed by satisfaction, the animal will connect that more firmly to the situation, so that when the context recurs, it will be more likely to do that action.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: And those actions accompanied by discomfort (these are Thorndike's words) will, other things being equal, have their connections with the situation weakened. I highlight that it's not just learning what to do, but associating situations with the behavior that leads to satisfaction, in Thorndike's term. So this has been called trial-and-error learning, and more modern takes call it instrumental or operant conditioning, terms that came much later. Intellectual and Educational Influences Now, in terms of my history, I was influenced by a lot of material, but among them were books that I discovered by accident. I may have been a high school student; I'm not sure. One was Introduction to Cybernetics by [William] Ross Ashby. It's a very understandable, clear book that just intrigued me, and I think that's the first place I saw the term "Cybernetics." Then a later book by Ashby, Design for a Brain, another very interesting, mathematically founded approach to brains. Then at some point I got [Norbert] Wiener's Cybernetics book. I didn't understand all of it, but it was intriguing and really set me off to study things related to this subject.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: In particular, I stumbled on a book by Michael Arbib, Brains, Machines, and Mathematics. At this point I didn't really know what direction to go, and this book sort of said, "Well, you don't need to choose. You can do brains, machines, and mathematics." So I became an undergraduate at the University of Michigan. I first majored in naval architecture and marine engineering. After one year I switched to math, for a number of reasons, but it was a good move. I majored in math and got a degree from Michigan in 1970. Arbib's book also introduced me to McCulloch and Pitts, who had written a paper called "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous [Activity]." This was the merging of logic and what, in those days, weren't called artificial neural networks but were neural networks similar to what one might find in the nervous system, and this was extremely exciting to me. That kind of sent me off. I applied to Michigan's graduate program, and I entered in 1970. It was a graduate program in computer science, one of the first, with a focus on biology and genetics and evolution. Computer science really wasn't a well-formed area back then.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: I joined and became a member of the so-called Logic of Computers group, where I was exposed to cellular automata, based on the idea of biological cells; to genetic algorithms, particularly John Holland, who created this optimization algorithm based on evolution [xx, yy]; and my advisor, Bernie Zeigler, had developed a theory of modeling and simulation. That was a kind of meta-theory of modeling, and it really influenced my thesis. Arthur Burks was a philosopher and an electrical engineer who participated in designing the first electronic digital computer. So it was a great experience in grad school. Adaptive Intelligence Research at Massachusetts I finished eventually, and in 1977 I became a postdoc at the University of Massachusetts, because I heard of a project funded by the Air Force called "Goal Seeking Components for Adaptive Intelligence." I thought, "Wow, that's really interesting." So I drove there and talked to Bill Kilmer. Michael was on sabbatical, and they hired me as a postdoc. That was my life for a considerable length of time after that. Michael [Arbib] is, of course, well known. He's written 40 books, perhaps, by this time, and he was an early cybernetician.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: Bill [Kilmer] had worked with McCulloch on a model of the brain's reticular formation. Nico [Spinelli] was a physician who was also interested in neuroscience. This group, and the center, which was called the Cybernetics Center for Systems Neuroscience, was my home there, as a postdoc [Otter[a] has "graduate student"]. So again, we see Cybernetics influencing all these people, and through them, me. The project was based on an idea by Harry [Klopf], who was a senior scientist with the Avionics Directorate of the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. He had the idea that neurons are individually hedonists that work to maximize some local analog of pleasure while minimizing some local analog of pain, and that intelligence was the result of the interaction of these self-interested agents. Today we would think of each of these agents as a reinforcement learning agent. He was the sponsor of this project. He worked for the Air Force but was not in the military, and he was able to get them to fund a project directed to seeing if his ideas, which were very iconoclastic, made any sense. Has this idea been around for a while, or is it new? Is it worth studying? So we worked on that.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: His idea, basically, is that neurons implement the Law of Effect, and that there is a signal that somehow encodes rewards or punishments to the neurons. We studied this, and again, this is “trial-and-error learning.” I also want to mention Rich Sutton. Sutton and I recently received the Turing Award for this work on reinforcement learning. Rich is now a professor in Edmonton, but Rich came as a student when I was a postdoc, and Rich and I worked together, along with some other students who joined the group over quite a few years. It was a wonderful period, because I didn't have to teach, and I didn't have to go to faculty meetings. We rewrote some proposals, but each one was for three years of funding. So it was an idyllic period of exploration, which unfortunately I think it is very rare to have the opportunity for now. The deliverables were reports, not devices. It was a rare opportunity. Reinforcement Learning's Early History I gave a talk some time ago called "In[b] the Beginning, Machine Learning Was Mostly Reinforcement Learning." This is a bit of history of reinforcement learning that we uncovered as we pursued the work on this project.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: Going way back, in 1933 there was an electromechanical device that actually learned, very simply by modern standards. Digital computers did not exist then. This was by Thomas Ross in the early 1930s, and then his student Stephen Smith built a mechanical rat that finds its way in a maze. It tries things, and if the path is blocked, it backs up and tries another path. He said this machine is better than a man or an animal at doing this, so it was a superhuman machine for finding its way through a maze, which of course was an instance of a type of problem that was not restricted to maze learning. This was 1935. Yes—

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect

The famous Alan Turing put this forward, although it was never implemented, because he didn't have access to the right computer back then. Computers came along a bit later, but this is a very clear statement of reinforcement learning. Then the first implementation of an artificial neural network on a digital computer was by Farley and Clark in 1954, and they trained it with reinforcement learning. I'll skip ahead. Well, it was a network containing what he called SNARCs, stochastic neural analog reinforcement calculators, and he wrote a paper in '61 that was very influential on me and Rich and our students.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: Of course, Marvin Minsky then really went in a different direction later, moving to symbolic methods, and the early connections to reinforcement learning and neural networks were considered not the way to go in artificial intelligence. Reinforcement Learning, Rewards, and Unintended Outcomes One interesting thing about reinforcement learning is that, as this diagram shows, the RL system generates actions, and they can influence almost anything that is not modeled. The critic then sees this and evaluates it. It doesn't need to know how it's produced or anything.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: A reinforcement learning system can learn how to get the critic to like what the system is doing without really knowing what's hidden inside it. This is a really interesting capability that can be exploited by using reinforcement learning systems. I should say that reinforcement learning is very slow compared to backprop [backpropagation], which is the algorithm used mainly for artificial neural networks. Reinforcement learning does the same kind of adaptation, but it estimates gradient information stochastically rather than computing it mathematically, which is what the backprop algorithm does. So RL is not the preferred method for training deep neural networks, because it's much slower. But I've always thought that it's much more plausible from a biological point of view. Now, finally, let's see. I'm probably out of time, but let me just say that with reinforcement learning systems, it's critical what the reward signal is, and in building these systems, that has to be designed in some way. There's a long history, even before computers, that if you're trying to maximize some performance index, you may not know what it's going to come up with.

speaker: Andrew Barto
section: Learning Paradigms and the Law of Effect
text: As Norbert Wiener, in fact, says, "Be careful what you wish for. You might just get it." You're not going to know a priori what it's going to be, and we're seeing that now. I don't know the interior mechanisms of these large language model agents, but they can do things that you didn't prepare for. It grants what you ask for, not what you should have asked for, or what you intend. Wiener used the story of the Monkey's Paw, the supernatural stories. King Midas, for example, is a classical example. He wanted things to turn to gold if he touched them. I think he touched his daughter or son, and they turned into gold, which was an unexpected consequence. And there's the wonderful movie Bedazzled, the old version. speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: [slide 1] Good. Okay. I should say I'm happily retired after several decades of work in neuroscience. [slide 2] What I'm going to talk about is a bit about the history of AI and Cybernetics as I see it, which is totally subjective on my part; then some differences between AI and Cybernetics, and commonalities; and then two paths not yet taken. And then, again, I'm going to reinforce what Andy said about the ethical problems that face us now. [slide 3] So, some preliminaries. This is the way I think about these things. Cybernetics is the science and design of purposive systems and their interactions, like conversations and power interactions. Purposive systems are natural and artificial systems that are organized so as to guide effective actions that realize internal goals. If they're autonomous, they have the freedom to choose those goals and the means to pursue them. Information, in the functional sense, is distinctions that switch the behavior of a system. Knowledge is information found by the system to be useful for attaining some goal.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: Again, that's a pragmatist conception of knowledge. Learning is a process of making distinctions and using them, and determining their efficacy in achieving some goal. And knowing, in this case, is knowing how: the ability to use knowledge to reliably attain a particular goal. Now, previous sessions, and I invite you to go back: [slide 4 / click here for readable PDF version of this timeline] we're not going to look at this slide, because it's impossible to read unless you blow it way up, but from session one there's a timeline of AI and Cybernetics. [slide 5] This would be my subjective map of all the different strands or paradigms that were going on. On one hand, under the rubric of symbolic AI, starting around 1956, you had symbols and rules, basically. Then you had a whole gamut of work on different kinds of trainable machines or machine learning: neural nets, trainable machines, classifiers, genetic algorithms. The Uttley machine was a conditional probability machine that is basically what big data and generative LLMs are using.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: Then adaptive feature selection, which was not part of the gamut in the beginning, but convolutional neural networks are more or less today's instantiation. What we call AI today is almost like the Republicans and the Democrats: they reversed roles. Symbolic AI was all symbols and rules. Today's scene is mostly machine learning of one sort or another, and statistical prediction. Then there were, coming out of Cybernetics, the earlier cybernetic traditions of the '30s and before: servos and feedback controllers. There were strands related to autonomous robots, self-organizing systems, bionics, reverse engineering of brains, human-machine learning, Management Cybernetics, and Social Cybernetics. Many of these strands, including machine learning, in my view, went out of business, or went underground, in the late '60s. This was because Marvin Minsky and McCarthy were given control of ARPA funding mechanisms, and they were vetoing pretty much anything that wasn't symbolic AI or programmable digital computers.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: But neural nets and trainable machines came back with the PDP risorgimento [Parallel Distributed Processing, often called connectionism] in the 1980s, and now we have deep learning and neural nets with millions of layers. I was a grad student at Binghamton. One of my beloved professors, Don Gause, who has now passed, had a course on adaptive programming in the early '80s, in '81, '82. There were no textbooks other than a textbook from the '60s on trainable machines, and so I lived through the dark ages of neural nets and trainable machines. Biological Construction and Adaptive Machines [slide 6] As I said, I consider myself spiritually a theoretical biologist, and I was thinking about the fundamental differences between biological systems and the machines that we build. One of them is that in biology, the organisms and lineages construct themselves, and they construct themselves adaptively, because they're under selective pressure to survive and reproduce. So there can be wholly new kinds of functions. The development of a new sensory system is a prime example, and these are emergent, in the sense that you would not have predicted before they appeared that they would be possible.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: Whereas the machines I was looking at had fixed features and fixed adaptive processes. They were operating within a space of definable combinations of features and actions, or features and classifications. [slide 7] So if you step back and look at percept-action machines that are connected to their worlds through sensors and effectors: they have the ability to change the internal coordinative part, which I called computation, because we were trying to formalize this whole percept-action loop. Now I would call it coordination, and that's what nervous systems do in organisms. You can have processes of steering, but you can also have processes of construction, where the hardware of the system is constructed. [slide 8] One can think about computers that are not connected to their environment except by symbols that people put into them; fixed robots that are connected in a fixed way to their environments; adaptive robots and adaptive machines that are connected to their environments via sensors and effectors, and that evaluate performance and then reorganize themselves, reorganizing the coordinative part in order to perform better.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: And then there can be adaptive self-construction, which I termed Evolutionary Robots back in the '80s. [slide 9] So the two ideas here, two types of adaptivity, are feedback to software and feedback to hardware. What I labeled adaptive systems are ‘feedback to software‘—they're operating within a space of features and decisions, possible actions. And evolutionary machines have ‘feedback to hardware’, where you're actually creating a new space, creating new primitives. Today I'll give some examples. Immune systems are a prime example. Biologicals are a prime example. [slide 11] [Gordon] Pask’s device, where he had an electrochemical assemblage, in the late 1950s, in which they steered the growth of iron threads in a ferrous sulfate solution, such that they could become sensitive to other aspects of their environments. And so this was sort of the first evolutionary construction of a sensor. Cybernetic Foundations and Unpursued Paths [back to slide 10] Now, going back to symbolic AI versus Cybernetics (I'm not going to go through this whole [slide]) but basically the guiding epistemologies and ontologies of symbolic AI are Platonic. They're focused on logic and reasoning.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: They think that symbols can be described and manipulated independent of their material substrates. Whereas Cybernetics was more or less inspired by the biology, neuroscience, and psychology of organisms that are embedded in material environments and trying to cope with acting within them. [slide 12] So, let's see. All right. Again, we'll do another path not taken. Evolutionary robotics really hasn't been pursued. I'm not sure it's a good idea at this point to pursue any new kinds of visionary machines, but that aside. Neural Timing and Signal-Centric Models [slide 13, 14] Since 1990, I've been working on neurophysiology and neurons. It turns out that neural codes are not exactly what people make them out to be. It's not how much, how often neurons fire, but the time patterning of the firing. This is in the auditory nerve in response to a pitched complex tone stimulus, and you can see that the neurons are locking onto the time pattern of the stimulus. That means there is an iconic, analog representation of the world in the temporal firing patterns of neurons. So I think of brains as self-production systems of interacting neural signals. It's a signal-centric view.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: They're time-correlation machines in which there are multiplexed temporal spike codes, in the time domain. Janet Baker, my collaborator, and I are thinking about neural time-domain, holograph-like representations and recovery processes, retrieval processes. To do this we're thinking in terms of neural time-delay nets and neural timing nets, which I proposed circa 2000 [date unclear in the recording][d]. The idea is that you have these signals. The signals have structure. The set of signals that is reverberating and being actively regenerated within central circuits and local circuits constitutes the contents not only of consciousness but of working memory. There are some other things, like bio-robot hybrids and self-reproducing robots, and I shout out to Jordan [Pollack] at Brandeis, and concept formation, which has still not been developed. AI Ethics and Autonomous Weapons [slide 17, 18] Now, what would a talk be without some doom and gloom today? We recently revisited the film Colossus: The Forbin Project. I recommend it. It deals with arrogant scientists putting AIs in control of weapon systems, in this case nuclear weapons.

speaker: Peter Cariani
section: Cybernetics and the History of AI
text: And just this week, [US TV journalist Rachel] Maddow reported that U.S. and Russian diplomats are now agreeing to allow fully automated control of weapons with no humans in the loop. So, we live in interesting times. Finally, just to echo what Andy said, the human use of technology and ethics for autonomous technologies. [slide 19, 20] Of course, Norbert Wiener: we need to go back and look at The Human Use of Human Beings. There are side effects of automation, but virtually all of them are failures of humans, in the use of these very powerful devices by humans: unexpected consequences, abdication of control, empowering malefactors and criminals, concentration of wealth, and usurpation of power. I think we can control AI if we collectively choose to do so, but that's a social consensus problem and a political problem, and we've had some successes in the past, but a lot of failures as well. So I think that we need a machine "Ten Commandments," to expand on Asimov's three laws of robotics, but leaving out the third law, self-preservation. So that's it for me. I've got references [slide 21+]  in case anybody wants to go look at those. But anyway, that's it.
